As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing "YMCA" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.

Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.

First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.

The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.

The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.

Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.

Demonstrators hold signs during a protest against U.S. President Donald Trump's visit to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit and related meetings in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Firdia Linsawati/AP hide caption
About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.
They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.

"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.

Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.

But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
"Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said.

When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.

Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

items.title: Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers are revealed?
paragraphs: Uefa has finally identified a candidate to take on Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

Less than 48 hours before Wednesday night's deadline, European football's governing body announced that French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo had received the unanimous support of its executive committee.
A late and surprise choice, Diallo said, "I think I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative."
But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he had the credibility and unifying potential to be able to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.
But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.
So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?
An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.
In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.
According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."
Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer", he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."
They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."
McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.
"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."
Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different when the heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".
Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered some setbacks.

Uefa called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, and then potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stand for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by £2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.
"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.
"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."
So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

So far, the legal action has not appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond football too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said Infantino and FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But now, armed with extra powers, they could force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

Could Infantino even be ruled ineligible to stand? According to Portuguese lawyer Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - Infantino should not be allowed to be a candidate in the election as Fifa rules limit presidents to three terms. In 2022, Fifa's Council agreed that his first period in office - between 2016 and 2019 - should not count as he was effectively completing the remainder of Blatter's term after his resignation. But as Maduro has said, a national association or confederation would need to challenge this decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

Japan Football Association honorary president, Kozo Tashima, has announced his intention to stand, along with former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega. But with uncertainty over how much support either man will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.
A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

items.title: Ukraine critically damages Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia
paragraphs: Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation.

Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.

Writing on social media, the Ukrainian president described the attack as “a response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure”. He said it was the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.

“Our warriors gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective,” he wrote. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

Earlier, Russian forces struck ⁠two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone ⁠and missile attacks ​across Ukraine.

Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, using a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.
The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted on Telegram.
He added: “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from travelling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes.”

Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.

The Russian government convened an emergency meeting to assess the attack, after which one of the country’s deputy prime ministers, Marat Khusnullin, briefed Putin on the damage to the bridge, according to the Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
Peskov added that the bridge would be repaired and would be “even better than before”, in comments to the Russian newspaper Izvestia.

But pro-war Russian commentators acknowledged that repairing the bridge would be very difficult, warning that, unlike in 2022 and 2023, Ukraine now had the capability to strike floating cranes and repair crews.
“Even installing a prefabricated arch under such conditions would be a formidable challenge,” wrote the influential Rybar Telegram channel, with close links to the defence ministry.

Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They also pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”

The Ukrainian blogger Anton Gerashchenko pointed out that Putin personally opened the bridge in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. “The Kerch bridge stands as the primary symbol of the Russian occupation of Ukrainian Crimea and the embodiment of its illegal annexation. It is Putin’s flagship project,” he wrote.

He added: “For years, Russian authorities claimed the bridge was ‘the most protected facility in the world’. Consequently, every successful strike shatters the myth of the invincibility of Russian air defences – as well as the notion that Ukraine is incapable of reaching key targets deep behind enemy lines.”

Ukrainians celebrated on Tuesday with memes. The company Fire Point, which manufactures the Flamingo missile, posted a popcorn emoji. Other social media users shared video of “Kerch Bridge on Fire”, a popular song by Saint Javelin which has become an anti-Moscow anthem.

Russian military bloggers were gloomy. One, Russian Engineer, acknowledged the Ukrainian military operation to paralyse the bridge had been “perfect”. Hundreds of unmanned aerial vehicles distracted Russian air defences, he said, before a clinical strike by ballistic missiles.
The attack will further complicate supplies to Crimea, after a summer in which the peninsula struggled with fuel shortages and an intensifying Ukrainian campaign to isolate it from mainland Russia.

Ukraine has for months focused its strikes on the key transport routes supplying Crimea, particularly the so-called Novorossiya highway, a key logistics corridor linking the peninsula to Russia’s Rostov region through the occupied cities of Melitopol and Mariupol.

Russia had already sharply restricted traffic across the Crimean bridge. Moscow has largely stopped using the crossing for rail fuel shipments since the 2022 Ukrainian attack damaged the bridge and set a fuel train ablaze.
Rybar wrote that the latest strike would force Moscow to “completely overhaul” its supply routes to Crimea, shifting more traffic to the Novorossiya highway.
Russia would also have to step up the installation of protective netting along the route, Rybar added, lamenting that the measure had not been introduced in the spring.

Meanwhile in Kyiv, loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in ⁠the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.
Russian forces launched a ​series of attacks on bridges crossing ‌the river earlier this ‌month and in October.
A Russian missile attack injured three people ‌in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.

Russia’s defence ministry claimed ⁠on ⁠Tuesday its ​forces had ⁠carried out a massive ⁠overnight strike ​on ‌Ukrainian ‌military-industrial facilities, ‌transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the ‌Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The ministry ​said the strikes also ⁠targeted energy facilities, ​port infrastructure ​and ​vessels ​used ‌by ​Ukraine’s armed ​forces.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier on Monday that intelligence showed Russia’s military was planning strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday.
Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.

Zelenskyy also said on Monday ⁠that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys ​Steve Witkoff and ​Jared Kushner, as well as European ​representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.

Kushner ​said progress had been ‌made towards an ​agreement, though important ​challenges remain to end the war, which Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.

items.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
paragraphs: Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".

Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Singapore, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms. Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.

Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.

That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

items.title: Woman who accuses Russell Brand of rape says prison message 'upsetting'
paragraphs: A woman who has made allegations against Russell Brand has said she finds it "upsetting" and "really shocking" that he was able to claim he was innocent from prison, following his conviction for rape and sexual assault.

Speaking after the comedian's wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, Mia Latter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she found it "appalling" to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she said.
Latter, 37, who has alleged she was raped by Brand when she was 16, was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.
Brand is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being found guilty at Southwark Crown Court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women.

In recent years he has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following, including in the US. In the message read out by his wife on their show, Brand said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
Latter said the broadcast "was really shocking to me... it was appalling, frankly, it was upsetting to watch".
She said the woman who gave evidence in the trial "got their verdict, and for him to say, 'I'm innocent, I'm not guilty' - well, you are, you're a convicted rapist now. There's no arguing with that".
Downing Street said on Monday it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said that "prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims".
Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time.
She was one of six women who made allegations against him as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation in 2023. None of the women were involved in his recent trial.

In an interview with the Sunday Times this week, Latter said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

She has waived her right to anonymity in order to campaign for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in the UK that would make sexual relationships between 16 and 17 year-olds and adults illegal.

Latter told the Sunday Times the Crown Prosecution Service decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings. She told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.
Latter told Today a staggered age of consent could have stopped her relationship with Brand "dead in its tracks".
She said: "It would have 100% made a difference because my parents tried to stop the relationship.

"They tried to prevent me from seeing him... But if it had been a criminal offence for him to be having a relationship with me, none of the subsequent abuse would have ever happened because they would have been able to stop the relationship dead in its tracks."
Latter also told Today that she and the complainants in Brand's trial had been accused of being "money hungry".
She said she had initially been reluctant to speak out because "I knew that the audience that he'd cultivated over the past few years would come for me".
"It's a criminal trial, there's no money.
"Me talking to the Times, me talking to you, me doing any interviews, there's no money, there's not a penny. We're just doing this in the pursuit of justice."
But Latter said Brand had been "monetising all these platforms" during his trial by continuing to make videos that appeared with advertisements on social media.

items.title: More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6043086/nx-s1-10006177" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Millions of Americans are expected to travel for the holidays in the midst of cold and flu season. Thibaut Durand/Getty Images hide caption
More people are getting the flu than usual this fall, according to the latest influenza tracking numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

"Flu started a bit early this year, so it's out there and spreading," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. "So people who are thinking of Thanksgiving travel need to get their protection as quickly as possible."

The flu shot takes about ten days to reach its full efficacy, so there's still time to get one before Thanksgiving, Schaffner says. And the sooner someone gets it, the better – especially because people will be gathering in enclosed spaces for the holidays.
AAA predicts that this year, around 82 million people will travel more than 50 miles over Thanksgiving break, including 73 million by car.

Getting the vaccine doesn't mean someone won't get the flu – but it does mean they'll be less likely to wind up in the hospital from influenza-related complications. Those include pneumonia and secondary bacterial infections.
"It can strike a healthy person at any age and put them in the emergency room. Flu is like that," Schaffner says.
People at the highest risk are seniors, young children and people with underlying health conditions.
Schaffner also says not enough people are getting their COVID boosters.

"Somehow they think that COVID has disappeared," he says. "But the people who are admitted to my hospital with COVID are invariably people who are not up to date with their vaccinations, as with flu. That COVID vaccine helps keep you out of the hospital. It is still a threat. It hasn't gone away."

People should have no trouble finding available vaccines for the flu, COVID and the highly contagious respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, at their local pharmacies and health care providers' offices, says Claire Hannan, the executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, adding that vaccination season is in "full swing."

"Now is definitely the time to get vaccinated," says Hannan. "Influenza is circulating, people are traveling, people are getting ready for Thanksgiving, the holidays. And the best protection you can get is from the vaccine."

items.title: She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades
paragraphs: Ashley Baukman is an apprentice at The Electrical Trades Center in Columbus, Ohio. With the future of work uncertain, some college graduates are turning to the skilled trades for job security. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

COLUMBUS, Ohio — A few miles south of The Ohio State University, Ashley Baukman is wrestling with a piece of steel tubing, using only a manual tool called a foot pedal and her sheer strength to bend it 90 degrees.

This class in conduit bending at The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio is part of an apprenticeship program Baukman began in the spring. She's here in class one day out of every two weeks. Other days, she's out on construction sites, working under the supervision of journeymen electricians.
For the 36-year-old college graduate and licensed social worker, it's a new chapter — one she hopes will be the foundation of a long-term career.
Being the first in her family to graduate from college had been a point of pride for Baukman.
"I was like, 'Oh, I'm going to do this. I'm going to do it the right way,'" she says. "But it didn't really work out that way, and that's okay. You live and you learn."

Baukman bends steel tubing alongside other apprentices at The Electrical Trades Center, a training school that's funded through the collective bargaining agreement between the Central Ohio Chapter of the National Electrical Contractors Association and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 683. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

Now, as an apprentice, she's getting paid just over $25 an hour for time on the job and a stipend for days she's in class. Already, she's earning more than she was as a social worker and is set to nearly double her wage in just over three years. So far, she's finding the work engaging and rewarding.
"You can see a project to completion, and you can — 'Hey, I did that,'" she says. "It's been pretty fun."
With AI throwing into question the future of work and the cost of college higher than ever, apprenticeships in the skilled trades are having a moment.

Once pushed primarily to the non-college bound, apprenticeships are increasingly being seen as a compelling alternative to higher education for anyone curious about the trades. The earn-as-you-learn model, which combines coursework with on-the-job training, requires no prerequisites or prior work experience. Acceptance is generally based on contractor need.
Right now demand for skilled tradespeople — especially electricians — is up.

The construction boom fueled by data centers has contributed to the rapid expansion of The Electrical Trades Center. Enrollment has grown from 500 apprentices in 2022 to more than 800 today. Once a night school, they now hold daytime classes to accommodate the growth.

The Electrical Trades Center director Trent Parker has seen interest in their apprenticeship grow in recent years. "The word is out that college is not the only way to go, that there are other alternatives that can provide a living wage with benefits," he says. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

Baukman may be the only licensed social worker among the apprentices, but as a college graduate, she has plenty of company. Trent Parker, the center's director and an electrician himself, says several dozen currently enrolled have four-year degrees, and roughly 300 applicants have at least some college on their resumes.
While Parker hasn't tracked the share of college graduates in the apprenticeship over the years, he's confident it's rising as sentiment toward the trades has shifted.

Parker recalls a recruiting visit he made to a technical high school 16 years ago. The school's vice principal told him they were grateful for the visit because they needed more opportunities for students who were "flunking out."

Parker was taken aback at the comment. He had just started as the apprenticeship's instruction coordinator and was realizing how deep the misconceptions run, how little this vice principal knew about the rigors of the work. That's now changing.
"You know, we're looking for high performers," Parker says. "The same people that are going to be successful in college are the same people that are going to be successful here."
Apprentices take a quiz on wiring applications. Enrollment at the training school has grown from 500 apprentices in 2022 to more than 800 this year. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption
He notes that the apprenticeship's curriculum is equivalent to college-level coursework. Conduit bending is based on trigonometry. Apprentices have to be able to manipulate decimals and fractions.

Parker was thrilled when in 2023, Ohio's governor signed into law a requirement that licensed school counselors visit a training center like this one to learn about apprenticeships and the careers they lead to, a major step in changing the "college or bust" mentality and recruiting more broadly into the field.
When his own two daughters were deciding about college, he encouraged them to consider following in his path.
"I asked them several times, 'Are you sure you don't want to be an electrician?'" he says. "Now I get to log into their Sallie Mae loan accounts and — you know — ugh. I agreed to pay what?"
First-year apprentices practice bending conduit, a task based on trigonometry. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption
Gather together some of the college graduates at The Electrical Trades Center, and you hear similar themes. A common one: Careers they pursued after college just didn't pay enough.

After finishing her degree in social work, Baukman found jobs in local government agencies working with children and seniors but never earned enough to support her blended family. Her last job was as a prevention specialist in schools, but what she really wanted to do was to become a school social worker, a role that requires a master's degree. With five children at home, plus an estimated $80,000 in student loans, she couldn't figure out how to make it work.
"It just wasn't in the cards," she says. "So I was looking for a change."

Mike Hansen entered the apprenticeship after completing college, ten years in the Army, and some graduate school. He was originally on track to do a doctoral degree in sport and performance psychology, but had seen how others who had gone into academia had struggled.

Apprentice Mike Hansen, a military veteran, pursued a career in academia but left before finishing his Ph.D. He now wishes he could go back and tell his teenage self to consider a career in the trades as an alternative to college. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption
"They were doing 40 hours of teaching and zero hours of research for $40,000 a year," he says. He left school after finishing his master's degree.

Now, at 39, he wishes he could go back and tell his 17-year-old self to consider a career in the trades from the start. The opportunity was there. His father was an airline mechanic and a member of the Teamsters union. His high school had a vocational school attached to it, but going there was highly stigmatized.

"I distinctly remember as part of our generation... it was massively looked down upon. You were considered a burnout," he says. "Guidance counselors, teachers, my parents, everyone was like, 'Go to college, get an engineering degree. You'll make six figures.'"
For Michael Hughes, the message was slightly different. "The expectation was to get a four-year degree in some field whatsoever, and you'll be fine," he says.
He wasn't sure what he wanted to do, so he majored in English.

Michael Hughes was a college English major who dreamed of writing for TV and movies. Now as an apprentice, he appreciates the breadth of what he's learning and the chance to apply it immediately. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

"I had a pipe dream of, you know, writing for TV and movies," he says. After college, he did work for a time for the Geek Squad, mounting televisions and installing home theater systems, among other jobs.

Now, as an apprentice, he's been pulling wire, adding pipe, and replacing panels and fuses in a variety of settings including a police station, a paper mill, a sheet metal plant and an auto plant. He's appreciating the breadth of what he's learning and the chance to apply it immediately.
"It's almost like learning a foreign language by just going to that country and communicating, and then also taking classes and someone teaching you the proper conjugations of verbs," he says.

Apprentices are in class one day out of every two weeks. On those days, they're paid a stipend in line with what they earn on job sites. Wages start at $23 an hour and rise as the apprentices reach milestones for hours worked. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

Between new construction, commercial renovations and the data center buildout, electricians in Ohio are flush with work. With data center projects in particular, contractors are offering big incentives to get the jobs done quickly.
Parker has heard of projects paying $5 or $10 over the union-negotiated hourly wage. On other projects, all overtime is double time. There's even a rumor about triple time.
"There's some crazy money to be made out there," he says.

The apprentices are guaranteed a minimum hourly wage that starts at $23 an hour. There are built-in raises that come as they reach milestones for hours worked, topping out at $46 an hour. With overtime, many journeyworker electricians earn well over $100,000 a year, something the apprentices are looking forward to.

For now, these apprentices don't get to choose where they work. The program assigns them, based on contractor need. Harry Cekovich has been happy with his assignment at a solar field, where he's primarily running cables through rows of solar panels. There too, he's been picking up overtime while also collecting a $100 per diem. It's money he puts towards gas, although the site is less than an hour from his home.

After graduating from The Ohio State University, Harry Cekovich worked for a chiropractor and later got into massage therapy, something he continues to do on the weekends. During the week, he's been working at a solar field as part of his apprenticeship. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

Cekovich is the only one in the group who knows what it's like to earn six figures. For a time, the 34-year-old Ohio State graduate was making pretty good money as a massage therapist and a bartender.
"Granted, I was working 60, 70 hour weeks," he says. "Crazy, nonstop hours, so nothing too great, honestly."
None of those jobs came with benefits. Now, through the union contract, he has both retirement benefits and health insurance with no premiums.
"It's nice to be able to go to doctors and get checked up now," he says.
The proliferation of data centers in Ohio has sent demand for electricians soaring. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption
With all the data center construction around Columbus, it's a given that the apprentices will work on a data center at some point. Some are more excited about it than others.
"If it's true about them making double or triple time… I want to work at data centers exclusively," jokes Cekovich.

"There's enough concern and discussion going on right now about the harms that data centers cause," he says, citing their heavy energy and water use and the noise they generate. "Once I become a journeyman, and I'm allowed to pick my calls, I probably won't pick a job call for a data center, personally."

Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton has called for a "conditional moratorium" on new data center construction to ensure that developers cover their own utility costs, adhere to environmental standards and use union labor, among other things.
Whatever happens, Hansen expects there will be plenty of work at area hospitals, schools, commercial buildings and factories.

The apprentices are aware that the rapid buildout of data centers — especially hyperscale ones built to power AI — is a big reason the apprenticeship has been able to bring in so many recruits. At the moment, it accounts for about half the work in the school's jurisdiction.

"It kind of seems like it is, for better or worse, the way of the future," says Cekovich, adding that the proliferation of data centers influenced his decision to go into the electrical trades. "Are we contributing to the end of civilization with AI getting to be what it might become? Not totally sure."
Come what may, Hansen believes he and his classmates will be okay.
"I would like to see Chat GPT wire a three-way switch," he says. "We're still going to need electricians."

items.title: Do school cellphone bans work? New study says yes – but it's complicated
paragraphs: Ameriana Walker, a student in the Wyoming Area School District in northeast Pennsylvania, demonstrates how a Yondr pouch works in September 2025. Jason Ardan/Citizens’ Voice via Getty Images hide caption
Jason Ardan/Citizens’ Voice via Getty Images
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students' reading and math achievement. Now, new research suggests putting students' phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses.

"Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year," says Harvard University's Tom Kane, one of the new study's co-authors. "It's been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak."
Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That's a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement.
"That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did," adds Dartmouth College's Douglas Staiger, another co-author.

The study's authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. It was a joint effort between Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth and NWEA, a K-12 testing and research organization.

Kane, Staiger and their teams analyzed a nationwide sample of more than 3 million elementary-, middle- and high-school students over the past five school years, comparing the test scores in schools that adopted phone pouches to the scores at similar schools that did not.

Not only did strict cellphone bans appear to trigger small learning gains, the researchers say, those gains didn't seem to fade out after the first year of implementation. Instead, Kane says, the gains appeared to continue, year after year – at least up to three years after adoption.
Tuesday's headline finding, that locking phones during the school day led to small but statistically significant improvements in math and reading scores, comes with an important caveat:
A separate study, from April, found that these pouches had "close to zero" impact on student test scores – and if there was a benefit, it was not statistically significant.
"Overall, we didn't find evidence of meaningful achievement gains," says Brian Jacob, a co-author of that April study and a professor of education policy at the University of Michigan.
What should we make of these seemingly contradictory results?
Both are large-scale studies by well-respected teams of researchers. The April study has been peer-reviewed; the more recent study has not.

Both studies similarly focused on schools' adoption of lockable pouches made by the for-profit company Yondr. According to Tuesday's paper, more than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the '19-'20 and '25-'26 school years. Typically, schools that use the pouches require that students put their phones in them at the beginning of the day and don't get them back until the end of the school day, when the pouches are unlocked by a school administrator with a special magnetic device.

But the two studies also differ in key ways. The April study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while Tuesday's study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.
Simply put, the study released Tuesday had more fine-grain, student-level data, but the study released in April was able to examine a much larger sample of schools.

But the two studies' findings also aren't as different as they may seem. Jacob and his co-authors did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math. It's just that those gains were offset by ban-related learning losses in middle school.

Overall, Jacob says, the new study "is encouraging. And if [the benefit] really persists and accumulates over time, it really could be a meaningful benefit. I think we'll just have to wait and see if that happens."

Another co-author of that April study, Tom Dee, a professor at Stanford University's Graduate School of Education, says of Tuesday's findings, "I hope they are right that these very small test score gains will aggregate and add up over time. However, I'm not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans."
Taken together, Dee says, he considers the results from these early studies into cellphone bans "largely disappointing," and insists "we need continued study on this topic."

Kane sees the results differently. Even if the benefit is small, he argues, relative to the cost – roughly $25 per student – these pouches still make financial sense for schools. "That's still a lot less than having to pay teachers for an extra week or two of instruction."
For nearly a quarter-century, from 1990 to 2013, math achievement among fourth- and eighth-graders rose steadily. Reading scores also improved.

Then around 2013, student test scores began a sustained tumble that continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and has only recently begun to slow. For years, politicians and pundits blamed pandemic-era school closures for the losses, but the data tells a different story.

"Particularly in reading, test scores were going down for four to six years before the pandemic," Stanford University researcher Sean Reardon told NPR earlier this year. "In fact, you wouldn't really know there was a pandemic effect if you just looked at the last 10 or 12 years of test scores. There's been just a steady kind of decline regardless of the pandemic."
Which raises the question: What happened around 2013?
Possible explanations abound. The federal government began stepping back from holding schools accountable for low test scores. Many schools also saw funding cuts in the wake of the Great Recession.
This new study is the latest to make the case that the mass adoption of cell phones by children and teens also helped fuel those test score declines.

The researchers note that, in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did. And similar rates in other industrialized countries coincided with similar student achievement declines.
Now, Kane says, he wants to study students' smartphone and social media use outside of school.

items.title: Ukraine strikes major Russian bridge with drones and missiles as aerial attacks escalate
paragraphs: FILE - A freight train runs on rails of a railway link of the Crimean Bridge connecting Russian mainland and Crimean peninsula over the Kerch Strait not far from Kerch, Crimea, on Monday, July 17, 2023. AP Photo//AP hide caption

A Ukrainian drone and missile attack prepared over several weeks struck a vital Russian rail and road bridge to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, in a stunning blow after nearly five years of war.

Zelenskyy portrayed the "unprecedented" operation on the Kerch Bridge as a masterstroke, as Ukrainian forces gradually wore down Russian air defenses before bombarding the prized target with missiles and drones overnight.
He didn't detail the damage but unconfirmed media reports said that a span of the bridge collapsed in the attack, in what would be an embarrassing setback for Moscow.

The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that traffic across the bridge has been halted and urged people "to refrain from trips in the direction of the bridge." He didn't mention any damage.

The Kerch Bridge is a crucial link in moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea and to support troops on the front line. The construction of the bridge, a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014, was inflammatory for Ukrainians.
Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.

A recent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022.

U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to talk about the war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China this week.
The Kerch Bridge attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, Zelenskyy said on social media.
Ukrainian forces knocked out defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other designated targets before launching Monday night's final attack, he said.

Domestically developed long-range drones struck the bridge's road section during the night while Ukraine's Neptune missiles and other drones aimed at the rail section, he said. Flamingo precision-guided missiles delivered the final blow, he said.
Russia's Investigative Committee said that the bridge was attacked by drones on both days and sustained damage. It didn't elaborate on the extent of the damage.
Zelenskyy noted that Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said.
Russian air defenses downed 1,441 drones during a second straight night of major Ukrainian attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
On Monday, Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war.

Elsewhere, authorities in Bashkortostan, a Russian region in the south of Russia's Ural Mountains, said that defenses repelled a "massive" drone attack on industrial zones of the cities of Ufa and Salavat. All plants there worked as usual, and no critical damage has been inflicted on them, officials said.

Independent news outlet Astra, however, reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refining and petrochemical complex, located nearly 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) east of the Ukrainian border. The complex has been attacked a number of times before.
In Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that around 800 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight. Most were downed far away, and 321 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital.
Experts are inspecting Kyiv's North and South bridges, damaged in a Russian ballistic missile attack, to assess the extent of the destruction, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Tuesday morning.

Russian attacks damaged other infrastructure and started fires in four districts of the Ukrainian capital, officials said, as Moscow continues its campaign to make life difficult for Ukrainian civilians.

The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces overnight carried out a major strike using land- and air-based precision weapons and drones on Ukraine's military industrial facilities, energy, transport and port infrastructure, as well as vessels used for Ukraine's armed forces.

Russian forces launched a combined attack on industrial facilities in three districts of the southern Ukraine region of Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18 others and leaving a large number of consumers in the region without power, said Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration.

Meanwhile, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the United States, and European partners held a working video call on Monday, during which they discussed the results of recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, and the agenda for the next stage of negotiations, said Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service.
"We aligned our positions and our next joint steps," Umerov said on Telegram following the conversation.
On the European side, representatives of France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, NATO and the European Commission joined the conversation.
The United States was represented by envoys Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and Alexus Grynkewich, the commander of U.S. forces in Europe, Umerov said.

items.title: More than £160m needed to clean up one of Europe's largest illegal dumps
paragraphs: The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land
ByMike McBride and Davy WilsonBBC News NI
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.
"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.
"I am pushing ahead with real enthusiasm with this."
Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.
Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.
One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.
